blocks.raw: <Note>The iron frame fundamentally changed how architects could design: walls no longer need to be massive to support weight. Curtain walls (thin exterior layers) could be supported by the frame. This separation of structure and skin enabled the skyscraper as a building type.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Critical distinction: Sullivan did NOT reject ornament—he rejected ornament that disguises function. His buildings are often richly ornamented, but every detail aligns with vertical piers or horizontal spandrels. The **Guaranty Building** is covered in terracotta ornament, yet it expresses vertical structure. Do not confuse "honest function" with "no ornament."</Warn>

<ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Structural Recognition**
Questions ask you to identify iron and steel frame construction in building diagrams or photographs. You distinguish iron-frame buildings (columns and beams visible or implied) from earlier load-bearing masonry. You explain why frame structure allowed greater height and required less exterior wall material.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Vertical Expression**
Questions show photographs of skyscrapers and ask why vertical lines dominate the composition. You explain Sullivan's principle: piers express vertical structure, spandrels separate floors, the overall composition is vertical because the building IS vertical stacking. You contrast this with later buildings that disguise vertical stacking with horizontal bands.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Form Follows Function**
Questions ask what "form follows function" means in skyscraper design. You explain: the exterior should express the building's purpose and structure, not reference historical styles. The function is floor-stacking; the form is vertical bay repetition. You distinguish this Chicago approach from European Beaux-Arts eclecticism.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <Callout>The LEA tests your understanding of the **Chicago School** (1880–1910) as the birthplace of the modern skyscraper. Questions focus on structural innovation (iron and steel frames, curtain walls), key architects (**Louis Sullivan**, **William Le Baron Jenney**), and the architectural principle "form follows function." You must understand why Chicago became the innovation center and how the skyscraper defined American modernism.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating Chicago School as purely American. Students ignore that European architects had developed frame structures and tall buildings (Paris, London). Chicago's innovation was *systematic* application: the frame skeleton became the design principle, not an incidental structure. Chicago unified technology, economics, and aesthetic philosophy.", "Forgetting about curtain walls. Students focus on frame and ignore the outer walls. The curtain wall—thin masonry or glazing supported by frame—is integral to the skyscraper concept. It's lighter, faster to install, and allows flexibility in plan. Say \"frame and curtain wall system.\""]} />
